title: Planet Orbitz
lede: Orbitz was designed as a novelty and sold like one: fast, then not at all.

chapters.title: “A lava lamp you can drink”
chapters.cap: cases sold by the end of 1996, by the company’s account
chapters.body:
Clearly Canadian, then nine years old and known for flavored sparkling water, launched Orbitz in 1996.[^1][^4] It used “fluid-gel” technology to keep small balls of gellan gum suspended in non-carbonated fruit drink, in flavors such as raspberry citrus and blueberry melon strawberry.[^1] The company aimed it at 12- to 17-year-olds and talked about a “Jetsons mentality.”[^1]

The Associated Press called it “a lava lamp you can drink” and, less kindly, “fruit-flavored phlegm in a bottle.” A product consultant called it potentially “the pet rock of the beverage industry.”[^1] The company reported better-than-expected sales: a million cases by the end of the year.[^1]

Science World reported that October that Orbitz had been introduced around the country the previous May.[^9] By July 24, 1996 a University of Arizona summer newspaper had listed it among the summer’s test-market launches, a non-carbonated, fruit-flavored drink with colorful floating spheres.[^11]

The press treated it as a stunt. Katie Couric tried it on NBC’s Today; her first reaction, by AP’s account, was “Ugh. Why?” and she later pronounced it a little interesting.[^1] BevNET, an early web beverage-review site, called it “just the strangest thing we have ever seen” in a review quoted by AP, and the marketing analyst Al Ries said beverage makers were getting desperate.[^1]

chapters.title: A liquid that holds a bead up
chapters.cap: yield stress of the liquid, measured by Minnesota rheologists
chapters.body:
Floating a gel ball in a drink is harder than it sounds. A patent application that Bush Boake Allen Inc. filed on October 25, 1995, titled Method of suspending inclusions, starts from the problem. Solid pieces in a beverage tend to sink to the bottom or float to the top, it says, especially when they are larger than about one cubic millimeter.[^12] The sources we opened do not say whether that patent covers Orbitz.

Jesse Wolff, a chemical engineer who helped develop Orbitz, told Science World that the liquid was what scientists call a fluid gel, made from ingredients similar to those in Jell-O.[^9] The magazine left a bottle alone for a few days. The spheres moved gradually down through the liquid but never sank to the bottom, and William Chalupa, a fluid-gel expert, conceded that gravity does indeed act on Orbitz.[^9] Shaking the bottle spread the matrix particles out and the spheres suspended again.[^9] A William F. Chalupa is also named as an inventor on the patent; we could not confirm that the two are one person.[^9][^12]

Rheologists put numbers on it. In August 1997 two participants in a University of Minnesota short course asked the instructors how gel-like particles, some as large as 5 mm across, stay suspended in the commercially available drink.[^10] P. Dontula and C. W. Macosko answered in the January 1999 issue of the Rheology Bulletin. Creep measurements gave the liquid a yield stress of 0.04 Pa, close to the 0.045 Pa from oscillatory tests and about twice what is used to suspend insoluble builder particles in liquid detergents.[^10] At a shear rate of 100 per second its viscosity was only four times that of water, which explains why it looks fluid at first sight. For particles 5 mm across, the largest density difference the liquid can support is about 12 kg/m3.[^10]

The paper adds that the liquid appears to have the consistency of water even though the suspension is stable to violent agitation.[^10] The authors used the measurements as a home exercise in a course, and learned that another professor had used the sample as a teaching example at the University of Michigan.[^10]
chapters.artCaption: Original illustration of a gel ball held in a liquid by a web of fine strands. Not to scale; not an official Orbitz asset.

chapters.title: Hot with teenagers, panned by adults
chapters.cap: Orbitz sales in the first half of 1997
chapters.body:
By 1997 it came in four flavors and sold for about $1.09 for a 10.14-ounce bottle, at 130 calories. The Spokesman-Review’s adult tasting panel gave it two stars; the only higher score came from a 13-year-old.[^2] The Washington Post reported that Orbitz had “captured a niche market among young people.”[^3]

Sales in the first half of 1997 were $9.4M.[^4]

Canada followed. On April 14, 1997 Clearly Canadian announced the Canadian launch of what it called North America’s first “texturally enhanced” alternative beverage, with sales from May 1 at accounts such as 7-Eleven, Shoppers Drug Mart and Famous Players cinemas.[^8] The campaign theme was “Defy Gravity. Get into Orbitz.”[^8] In the Washington region the exclusive distributor, Atlantic Beverage Co., had carried Orbitz for six weeks. Its president, Bill O’Leary, said Orbitz was “moving very well” after that time. To handle the added work, the company had moved its beverage operations to a Jessup plant nearly double the size of its old distribution site.[^3]

Douglas Mason, then president and chief executive, called the consumer response to the U.S. launch “overwhelmingly positive” and said the company planned to extend Orbitz to the United Kingdom, Australia, Sweden and selected Asian countries in 1997.[^8]

chapters.title: “Orbitz is still weird. It’s just not new.”
chapters.body:
In the first half of 1998 Orbitz sales were $1.46M. Clearly Canadian’s vice-president of marketing, Jonathan Cronin, said: “Orbitz is still weird. It’s just not new in 1998. We weren’t expecting Orbitz to sell in 1998 what it sold in 1997.”[^4] The company had no immediate plan to discontinue it, and moved on to an energy drink and an oxygenated water.[^4]

By 1999 Orbitz had been discontinued.[^5]

The rest of the record on the decline is thin and partly secondary. Strategy reported that, despite what it called feeble Orbitz sales, the company’s overall net profitability was improving.[^4] A company-history reference says a patent suit that Bush Boake Allen, which had supplied raw materials for Orbitz, brought against Clearly Canadian was settled in May 1998 with a licensing fee. It dates a buyback of distribution rights in several key Mid-Atlantic states to June 1998, and says sales of Orbitz were suspended, with a significant writedown, in its account of the fall of 1999.[^13] We found no court record of the suit, and no primary source gives the date Orbitz production ended.

The maker’s later annual reports put the decline in context. The U.S. new age beverage market grew from $3.8B in wholesale dollar sales in 1992 to an estimated $13.1B in 2002, Clearly Canadian’s annual report for 2002 said, citing Beverage Marketing Corporation, while the company’s own revenue fell.[^6] The same report warned that the lifecycle of a beverage brand may be limited to a few years in a distribution area, and that distribution companies once independent of the traditional soft-drink makers were less willing to distribute other companies’ new age beverages.[^6] Its Competition section names Hansen Natural Corp., a producer of natural sodas, smoothies, functional drinks, juices and iced teas.[^6] Hansen’s own annual report for 2002 shows net sales that rose in every year from 1998 to 2002.[^20]

chapters.title: From Planet Orbitz to Orbitz, LLC
chapters.cap: orbitz.com shows a domain-service placeholder, between the drink’s site and the travel company’s
chapters.body:
The drink had its own corner of the early web. The April 1997 Canadian release said the address of the Planet Orbitz site, www.orbitz.com, was prominently displayed on all Orbitz packaging, and described comics by the syndicated artist Dirk Van Stralen and a tour of an Orbiterium spaceship.[^8] A capture saved by the Internet Archive in December 1997 is a prelude page that invites visitors to set gravity aside and tour the Orbiterium, with one route for Netscape and another for Internet Explorer; a capture from January 1999 shows the same prelude.[^35]

By February 2000 the address showed a domain-service placeholder saying the domain was registered by a member of myinternet.com.[^35] The airline-backed travel venture, announced in November 1999 as T2 and incorporated on February 24, 2000 as DUNC, LLC, was officially named Orbitz, LLC and Orbitz, Inc. in July 2000, according to a company-history reference.[^14] A capture from January 2001 says that soon the difference will be clear, beside a notice of ©2000 Orbitz, LLC, and by May 2001 the page advertised a search of all airlines and over 2 billion fares.[^35]

No source we opened says how or when the address passed from the drink to the travel company, or whether Clearly Canadian sold it. The captures cited here show the before and the after; the change itself is not documented.

chapters.title: Collectors’ bottles
chapters.cap: about what an unopened 1990s bottle can fetch on eBay
chapters.body:
Clearly Canadian’s total revenue fell from $34.9M in 1998 to $20.5M in 2002, and it lost money every year from 1999 to 2002.[^6] In 2015 a company representative said fans still asked for Orbitz constantly, but that it no longer had the equipment to make it.[^5]

Unopened bottles from the 1990s sell to collectors for around $50.[^5] The balls do not always stay up: in a 2012 photograph of an old bottle they have sunk to the bottom.

The name outlived the drink on paper. The maker’s annual report for 2005 still cited Orbitz among the innovative products it could draw on, and its report for 2006 listed Orbitz among the products it had historically introduced.[^17][^18] In a November 2005 press release the company described Orbitz in the past tense, as a drink with gel spheres that seemed to defy gravity.[^26] On September 29, 2006 it applied to register ORBITZ with the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office for soft drinks, non-carbonated fruit-flavored beverages and energy drinks. The office published the application on February 12, 2008 and issued a notice of allowance on May 6, 2008; in December 2008 it recorded the application as abandoned because no statement of use or extension request was filed in time.[^22] A different applicant, an individual, filed ORBITZ DEFY GRAVITY DRINK ORBITZ for beverages on March 5, 2014 and abandoned it on request on May 9, 2014.[^23]

Fast Company reported in October 2024 that the old owners sold the trademark and that the machine that made the Orbitz spheres broke down and was sold off for parts; it did not name a buyer.[^24] Clearly Canadian itself came back, by the same article’s account: production stopped around 2010, Robert R. Khan acquired the company in 2012 and full-scale production resumed in 2017.[^24]
